text: Roles, ACLs, scripted conditions, SSO, MFA — everything so far controls who can reach data and how they prove who they are. None of it changes one fact: once a value is written into a field, ServiceNow itself can read it. For a small set of truly sensitive fields, some organizations need a stronger guarantee than that.

Edge Encryption places an encryption proxy inside the customer's own network — the same spirit as the MID Server pattern from the Integrations course. Sensitive field values are encrypted on the customer's side of the network boundary, before the request ever reaches ServiceNow's cloud. Only ciphertext ever arrives at ServiceNow's servers.

The practical result: ServiceNow's own platform and support staff never have access to the plaintext of an Edge-Encrypted field. Only the customer's own environment holds the keys and the real value. That's stronger than a promise not to look — the capability to look is never even present on the vendor's side.

Column-level encryption is a simpler, related idea: encrypting specific fields at rest in the database, protecting against storage-level exposure like a stolen backup. It doesn't require a customer-side proxy, and the application layer still decrypts the value during normal processing — a narrower guarantee than Edge Encryption's.

Encryption isn't free. An encrypted field's plaintext isn't readable by the platform, so full-text search won't find matches inside it, reports that aggregate on the real value stop working meaningfully, and some integrations behave differently. Every field you encrypt trades platform functionality for confidentiality.

So encrypt deliberately: identify the genuinely sensitive fields that truly need this protection, and leave the rest of the instance working normally. Blanket-encrypting fields to be safe quietly breaks search, reporting, and automation for little real benefit on fields that weren't sensitive to begin with.

Encryption protects a value's confidentiality. Next, we'll look at a different kind of data protection: anonymization and masking, which change how sensitive data looks to different audiences rather than how it's stored.
